identity.title: Patient taps out the palpitation rhythm: regular vs irregular; rapid regular vs 'skipped beats'

technique.how: Ask the patient to tap the rhythm of an episode on the table or their chest with a finger. Note whether it is fast and perfectly regular, fast and chaotic/irregular, or normal-rate with an occasional pause followed by a heavy beat ('skipped beat'). Compare with the rhythm you palpate or see on ECG if symptoms are present.
technique.prerequisites: Patient able to recall and reproduce the rhythm; works best soon after an episode.

interpretation.positive_finding: A rapid, metronome-regular tap pattern is the classic description of SVT or sinus tachycardia; a chaotic irregular pattern suggests atrial fibrillation; isolated pauses with a forceful beat suggest premature beats.
interpretation.negative_finding: An unremarkable or unreproducible tap pattern does not exclude arrhythmia; the 2009 RCE concluded the clinical examination cannot exclude significant arrhythmia in most patients.
interpretation.pitfalls: Patients' perception of regularity is unreliable, and rapid AF can feel regular; symptom-rhythm correlation on a monitor remains the reference standard.
interpretation.changes_what: Chaotic irregular pattern: obtain ECG/monitoring for AF and assess stroke risk. Regular rapid pattern: pursue SVT/VT work-up. Skipped beats with normal ECG: likely benign ectopy.

sources.citation: Thavendiranathan P, Bagai A, Khoo C, Dorian P, Choudhry NK. Does this patient with palpitations have a cardiac arrhythmia? JAMA. 2009;302(19):2135-2143.
Zwietering P, Knottnerus A, Gorgels T, Rinkens P. Arrhythmias in general practice: diagnostic value of patient characteristics, medical history and symptoms. Fam Pract. 1998;15(4):343-353.

Hoefman E, Boer KR, van Weert HC, Reitsma JB, Koster RW, Bindels PJ. Predictive value of history taking and physical examination in diagnosing arrhythmias in general practice. Fam Pract. 2007;24(6):636-641.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use the tapped rhythm to withhold ECG or monitoring in patients with syncope, chest pain, dyspnoea, or known heart disease.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: A rapid irregular pattern in a patient with stroke risk factors, or any pattern with syncope, warrants same-day ECG and rhythm documentation.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: No reproducibility data; the manoeuvre is a bedside teaching convention rather than a validated test.

extraction_notes: No study reporting the accuracy of a patient-tapped rhythm (regular vs irregular vs skipped beats) against ECG-documented arrhythmia was found. The 2009 RCE abstract (PMID 19920238) states that apart from neck pounding, cardiac-disease history, sleep/work context, panic disorder and duration <5 min, 'No other features significantly alter the probability of clinically significant arrhythmia'; its Table (paywalled) may contain a 'regular vs irregular' row that could not be checked. Zwietering 1998 (762 GP patients, transtelephonic ECG) and Hoefman 2007 (127 GP patients, 30-day event recorder) abstracts give only regression associations, not per-symptom accuracy. Searches: 'irregular palpitations atrial fibrillation symptoms diagnostic accuracy history' and 'palpitations history physical examination predictive value arrhythmia general practice'.
